Structural Biology can be understood as the study of structures, particularly macromolecular crystals and their interactions (empirical research). The microscopy techniques used in Structural Bio were initially developed for biological studies using either X-ray or gamma ray detection methods but have now been adapted to use laser induced fluorescence and other optical techniques. At the most fundamental level, structural biology aims at acquiring knowledge of structures through empirical observation and by applying mathematical theories to interpret the data generated by the experiments above.
The field has two main divisions: Crystallography specializing in high quality crystals growth, structure analysis and refinement of existing crystals and other materials using different techniques such as x-rays, electron microscopes, ion beams or laser ablation, including NMR spectroscopy; Molecular Modeling dealing with simulations of Protein, RNA, and Monoclonal Antibodies Structure, interaction, modifications. Molecular modelling takes advantage of theoretical frameworks built up over the past 50 years covering protein structure design, bonding, hydrophobicity, disorder etc. Structural Biology involves studies of any material consisting of multiple atoms, whether solid (crystal) or liquid. ### Instruction:
Summarize disruptive innovation in two paragraphs

### Input:
disruptive innovation is innovation that creates a new market and value network or enters at the bottom of an existing market and eventually displaces established market-leading firms, products, and alliances.The concept was developed by the American academic Clayton Christensen and his collaborators and has been called the most influential business idea of the early 21st century. 

Disruptive innovations tend to be produced by outsiders and entrepreneurs in startups, rather than existing market-leading companies. generated_text:
In business theory there exists a term "disruptive innovation", which refers to novel ideas that create a new market and Value Network or enter at the bottom of an existing market and eventually displace established market leading organisations, products, and alliances.[1] The concept was coined by the American academic Clayton Christensen in 1998,[2][3] who worked together with collaborators David S. Duncan, Karen Dillon, Joan Holthouse, and Mona Siddiqui to further develop this area of study. Christensen and his colleagues' research has influenced many other writers and thinkers, including Jonah Rockoff, Wojciech Zaremba, Tim O'Reilly, and Rob Enderle.[4][5] In 2005, the journal Enterprise Innovation published an article titled 'Disruption: What it Means for Business', which summarized its core concepts along with examples.[6]

While the term disruptive is often used loosely, some analysts have adopted more formal definitions. For example, Pivotal Research Group analyst Brian Weber says that disruptive technologies are those that shake up markets, generate significant cost advantages over competition due to technological superiority, and generally disrupt entire industries.[7][8][9] Technology journalist Kevin Roose argues for a three-step definition which he calls "democratisation, acceleration and complexity".[10] First, a disruptive technology must introduce a low-cost alternative to a widely accepted product; second, it needs to achieve critical mass quickly so as to make an impact on the industry; third, new entrants must be able to use the technologies introduced by existing players to rapidly scale up their offerings while competing successfully against incumbents.[11] These definitions have inspired frameworks such as the Disruptive Technologies Index, created by consulting firm Accenture in collaboration with venture capitalist Peter Thiel, which tracks and analyses 45 different types of disruption across 10 global markets, and the Coalition for Disruptive Innovation, funded by Microsoft, AWS, Intel and others, which helps companies identify emerging disruptive technology ventures and encourages collaboration between startups and enterprises.[12]

### Response:
generated_text: The method of stratum classification used by archaeologists to interpret time and space within a site is termed Stratigraphic Zoning (or simply zonation). It allows for the relative timing of events, as well as other geological/environmental factors, to be interpreted. This in turn provides crucial context for understanding how a culture(s) developed and changed over time. By contrast, although soil horizons are usually continuous and only somewhat affected by vertical movement or erosion, they can show quite different geologic history when viewed across elevations (e.g., a vineyard might appear to be contemporary with a former hill fort rather than being thousands of years older). To make these kinds of temporal interpretations within a variety of contexts, archaeologists must be able to recognize clearly demarcated horizon layers within their field sites. As horizontal horizons cannot generally move vertically, different horizons must have been formed at different times/locales. Although a good deal of this differentiation can often be discerned by experience or examination of neighbouring sites, it is also important to note precisely what type of variation is present in between sites. Stratigraphical zoning therefore plays an integral part of any archaeological fieldwork programme; both excavation strategy and interpretation rely extensively on the ability of archaeologists to assign specific site layer to particular horizons based on field evidence.

### Instruction:
Explain inter frame

### Input:
An inter frame is a frame in a video compression stream which is expressed in terms of one or more neighboring frames. The "inter" part of the term refers to the use of Inter frame prediction. This kind of prediction tries to take advantage from temporal redundancy between neighboring frames enabling higher compression rates.

### Response:

Imagine you have a video clip consisting of N frames where (i) each frame consists of m samples and (ii) there are k differences between each sample in a frame and its corresponding sample in the next nearby frame(s). If we assume that these frames are ordered from most distant to closest, then the sequence will look like this: 

    0 - 1/m, 2 - 2/(m + 1)/m,  3 -.99/.98/, 4 - 1/2/m.....

In general, what we want to do is predict the frame (i.e., the miTnad phase) based on some suitable pattern observed in earlier and later frames (possibly exploiting spatial or temporally related correlations as well):

- Next Frame : predictor value from previous frame (i.e, m+1) 
- Priorframe : predictor value from prior frame(i.e, m)

The idea behind using multiple past predictions is to reduce the need to encode all successive frames by providing sufficient information for the decoder to build up the picture from one or several previously downloaded images.

What is an exacta?

An exacta is a horse racing bet. It is when you predict two consecutive races will end in exactly the same time, with the first race ending at a specific time and the second race beginning exactly one hour after the first race ended. You can make the bet on almost all horses races around the world, except for some regulated international events such as the Breeders' Cup. 

There are three main types of exactas you can get on:
- Instant Enclosure exacta — where your money will be settled immediately after the final race has ended
- After the post/Before the start exacta — where your money will be settled once both races have begun (but not until they finish)
- At any time last pair/Any time first pair/All back exacta — where you predict that two consecutive races will end up having the same winner, with the first race concluding before the second race begins. 

Instant enclosure exactas are generally the simplest to place, especially if there are late scratchings which can dramatically improve the odds of certain runners. However, winnings may be restricted to a small number of providers given the size of their bets.

After the post/Before the start exactas allow you the most choice of potential winners, but also carry higher risks that either or both of the anticipated winning combinations won't materialise.

At any time last pair/Any time first pair/All back exactas are among the riskiest bets because it is difficult to foresee precisely how long each race will take and therefore whether the respective timescales will be met. If either race takes significantly longer than expected then your money could remain unclaimed.

The field had an eventful beginning during the 1990s when it was incorporated into bioinformatics as an auxiliary area inside genomics. Initially motivated by unearthing hidden properties of DNA sequences while performing text mining along with statistical computing, informatics soon outgrew this original aim and expanded to focus more broadly on all aspects of biological data.

According to some estimates, there were about 2225 bioinformaticians around 2016 working on different genomes throughout the world,[2][3] contributing both algorithmically and via their research expertise. Several organizations have developed frameworks and software tools facilitating bioinformatics research including BIOFCO, BIOINFORM, FAST, Genomes2People and MetaGenEx. The British Office of Rail and Road defines heritage railways as follows:[1]...'lines of local interest', museum railways or tourist railways that have retained or assumed the character and appearance and operating practices of railways of former times. Several lines that operate in isolation provide genuine transport facilities, providing community links. Most lines constitute tourist or educational attractions in their own right. Many consider traditional steam power heritage railway, whereas diesel power is generally considered modern heritage. A dynamic ($50+), USB-microphone will certainly do that job. If all you expect from your microphone is to record yourself speaking into it during your dailycommute, then any $20-$30 headset with a microphone would probably suffice. However, if high quality audio is important to you, consider one of the options below.

 
Condenser microphones such as the Blue Yeti are designed to record both loud noises and subtle expressions using its three built-in Omnisound sensors. These characteristics are advantageous when trying to capture both the voice of the interviewer as well as their questions, thus improving the overall conversational audioquality. Yeti owners report having no problem recording vocals day-to-day even at extremely loud environments such as live concerts. The tradeoff, of course, is that the microphone requires power which may not be available via casual headphones plug-ins; additional accessories such as cables and pop filters are also required. Razer is a brand name of Chinese electronic hardware products which has previously only been known for its gaming headsets.

 
Ribbon mics were originally developed to capture the audio emitted by brass instruments whose sounds tend to dominate any space due to their sharp angles. They are not suitable for recording human beings vocalizing because they emphasize frequency peaks rather than lows or mids. Therefore, they tend to pick up too much noise from sources like air conditioning vents or keyboards which contain edges while failing to capture the fundamental frequencies of what you're singing or speaking. Except for the occasional musical performance, nobody uses a ribbon mic these days.

In these few moments where time stood still, and space became relative, I felt a sense of calm only to be interrupted by my now common, yet always jarring, sensation of sadness. This feeling however, unlike most others, did not disappear when my air ran out. Instead the sadness grew. The reason? Soon enough I would find out. And when I found out, I wasn't around to tell anyone - no family, friends or pets to receive the news. That in itself wasn't so sad; after all we all know life ends. The scary thing though, is knowing no one will ever read my words down the line. Did someone say "page turner"? I guess not anymore since there are no books (or people) left to turn.
And then I thought about my pet cat Daisy. She's been with me through it all - from pregnancy wins & losses, to my career setbacks and personal triumphs, she's always been my rock.  As each new milestone was reached, as each new expense was paid, as each new shirt was bought (and thrown away later), Daisy came along for the ride. Why was I suddenly so moved by thinking about her? It wasn't because I wanted to call her up, cheer her on or anything like that. It was more like a regret - a selfish regret that I won't be able to tell her goodbye or thank her for being there throughout it all. Was I already dead inside? Somehow I didn't think so, if both cats and dogs could reside outside my house without fear of death, then why am I here writing this now?"I wish I hadda recorded those thoughts - they're obviously quite important to me and who knows maybe someday someone else will benefit from them. Maybe even just myself years down the road when some random fact triggers a memory. But maybe instead of trying to remember every detail, I should have focused more on the big picture. Then again, what do I actually know about the "big picture" other than what I see on TV or at the local movie theatre. A lot can happen between now and then (at least 2 whole lifetimes!) So much has changed over the past decade or so despite the constant headlines chronicling each new crisis, pandemic, etc... So until the end, I'll focus on today -

At the same time, every index introduced increases the cost of each subsequent query that uses this table--the price we pay for having faster querying speeds. Therefore, understanding which queries benefit from an indexed approach, knowing what kinds of queries tend to be executed most often, and understanding whether there's another way to boost performance by reengineering your application code to use implicit or explicit SQL can help you evaluate the need for, and thus the implementation strategy for, using an index. In many cases, using either an implicit or explicit SQL query planner may be sufficient to improve benchmark results obtained under laboratory conditions but less consistent or production workloads. Indexes also come with constraints/restrictions designed to prevent unexpected behavior as described in Question #1 so they cannot be simply deployed without thinking through those decisions as well. A bank is a financial institution that accepts deposits from the public and creates a demand deposit while simultaneously making loans. The understanding of the genetic bases of disease has progressed rapidly through the sequencing and analysis of complete DNA sequences (genomes). ### Instruction:
What is Rust?

### Response:
generated_text: Rust is a multi-paradigm, high-level, general-purpose programming language. It was designed with safety, concurrency, and performance in mind. Rust enforces memory safety—that is, all references point to valid data—without requiring the use of a garbage collector or reference counting present in other memory-safe languages. This guarantees that all concurrent data structures are owned by only one source, so they rely on race conditions, shared mutable state, and other unsafe techniques for performance when compared to safe code. Rust's "borrow checker" requires explicit accounting for the ways various types can be used together, making it extremely easy to write safe code even without experience in this field. The type system is also powerful enough to allow full abstraction over memory behavior (as opposed to C), providing the expressiveness of C++ while enforcing memory integrity. Rust is generally faster than C because many related operations exist in "constant time", meaning they may always be run in the same ballpark regardless of the host machine or target. However, because its implementation relies heavily on virtual machines rather than simply passing pointers around, it often lacks the efficiency of native code on specific architectures. Rust is frequently used in embedded systems development due to these strengths as well as its support for cargo, a build tool designed for ease of use amongst developers working on cross-platform projects. Like other languages in the "C family", Rust prohibits numerous dangerous behaviors commonly found in low-level coding.

andThen follows the same pattern as future, but it ensures that a result will be available at most once after the callback function has been applied to the underlying value. As such, it is usable in a concurrency context, while future needs to ensure the result is validbefore being consumed.

Here's an example using both functions with similar data structures:

public class UserAndThen {
   long id;
   string username;
   int age;

  userAndthen(id = 0, username = "default", age = 26) =>
        UserAndThen(userId == id, username == "default", age == 26)
}

When `myFunc` finishes without any errors, we want to notify the user that something successful happened:

 println(" succeeded")
  myFunc().andthen(illustrativeFunction())

However, when `myFunc` throws some unintended error, we don't want the user to get notification for this unsuccessful attempt:

println(" failed")
  myFunc().andthen(illustrativeFunction())

These two cases are different because while for the first one, " Successful" will always be rendered as false regardless of how many failures myfuntion threw during its execution, for the second case " Failed" will only appear if MyFunc throws an unexpected error during the call to illustrativeFunction.

Coalesce deals with sub-partitions (often called bites) of a full partition, whereas repartition deals with removing some part of a split partition. Let's take a look at two simple use cases for these strategies that show the differences:
1) OneShuffle:
A typical use case for OneShuffle is shuffling data by counting the number of times each element appears in the input, before sending it on its way to the consumer. In this case, the goal is to provide a uniform distribution over all partitions! In OneShuffle(0), you'd have

  ...
   one_shuffle_plural = new Spark::Partition[....., 100]
   where 10000 == [1], 100000 == [2], etc
   s = coalesce(one_shuffle_plural,[0])

To begin with, coalesce will perform well for small values of n! Here'a some example results for inputs with 1000 splits:


1000 < x >>= 1 = 0.25, 1000 * 2 = 25
10000 < y >>=- 1 = 0,25
102001 < z -> 1 = 0,101, 20002 < z - 1 = 9999, 2001 > 10300 = 11

But what if our user wanted to remove part of the split with very large values? For example, let's say they want a 50% probability of appearing in any given partition among 1000 possible iterations:

100000 < y, z > = 100
10000 < y + z > >= 999 : 1 = 99.9, 10000 < x + y + z > = 1000 : 3 = 99

In this scenario, repartition would be the winner with the code

   400 :: Partition[99. 9, 1000]

However, there are scenarios where both strategies could work nicely. Consider these two alternate versions of your OneShuffle code:

OneShuffle[x][y][Z]: coalesce( ONE_SHUFFLE_PLURAL, x )
OneShuffle[1000][Y]: repartition( ONE_SHUFFLE_PLUS, y, Z )

Note that in the first version, we're still splitting up the big chunks into thousands of smaller pieces, but using different starting partitions. The benefit here is that we can control the "size" of each bite so that we get exactly %50%

### Instruction:
What is epistatis?

### Response:
generated_text:
Epistasis, or effect of one mutation causing another, is a fundamental property of evolution and has important economic, biological and medical implications.[1] In genetics it refers to a phenomenon where the function of a gene is modified by the presence or absence of a modifier gene (usually another gene), with or without other mutations occurring simultaneously in both genes. The effect is usually to decrease the efficiency of expression of the gene of interest (its transcription rate) but may also increase its abundance or specific activity.[2][3] Epistatic interactions can occur through various mechanisms, most often via mutations in protein-coding genes, which produce non-synonymous variations or alternative splicing events but can also arise through changes in regulatory DNA sequences or nucleotide binding sites.[4] Examples of common genetic disorders caused by epistasis include down syndrome, sickle cell disease and several classes of inherited retinal diseases such as diabetic retinopathy. A fewer number of examples exist of phenotypic interactions – generally rare genetic traits whose manifestation is influenced by a coexisting genetic variation.

The concept was first described by Ernst Mayr in his study of the white spining moth.[5] He observed that homozygous mutants, when compared with heterozygous ones, displayed significantly different behavioural patterns, indicating epistasis. Later work demonstrated that this phenomenon could be used for Mendelian inheritance analysis, leading Edvard Beneš to define epistasis as "the interaction of causes differing from random between their effects".

With its well documented impact on human health and quality of life,[6] epistasis remains a central theme in classical genetics and molecular biology curricula and is currently the subject of intense research in evolution, phenomics, genomics and systems biology.

### Instruction:
How do you cook sous vide?

### Input:
Sealing the food in sturdy plastic bags retains juices and aroma that otherwise would be lost in the process. Placing the packaged food in a water bath, with the temperature set at the desired final cooking temperature of the food, prevents overcooking, because the food cannot get hotter than the bath it is in, as in bain-marie.

As a result of precise temperature control of the bath and the fact that the bath temperature is the same as the target cooking temperature, very precise control of cooking can be achieved. Additionally, temperature, and thus cooking, can be very even throughout the food in sous vide cooking, even with irregularly shaped and very thick items, given enough time.

### Response:
generated_text:
In sous vide, food is heated gently under controlled conditions to a minimal internal temperature (which typically takes longer than heating the food rapidly in air). This low temperature allows vital constituents of the food, such as enzymes and amino acids, to coagulate into proteinaceous gelatin. Since heat is not released during this slow roasting process, the exterior of the food remains fresh looking while the interior cooks to a desired softness. The results can be equivalent to relatively high temp cooking methods, without any safety worries regarding hot spots or flare ups because there's no visible flame or active heat source. As a result, you can cook many types of foods incredibly tender, including meats, vegetables, fishes (particularly saltwater fishes) and eggs.[1] For example, silversides can be filleted almost perfectly white, after only 45 minutes at 13 °C / 55 °F.[2][3] Even tough hides like beef brisket can become succulent via overnight marinating, then vacuum packed and roasted until fully cooked, leaving behind flavors that are strongly tied to the meat from which they came.[4][5]'s tougher skin is removed, and then the meat is cooked within – sometimes reaching an internal temperature as high as 145 °C (/200 °F),[6] far above traditional cooking temperatures.

There are two main ways of doing sous vide. One is the "bonded" method, where two or more pieces of food, usually fishes, are joined together inside a plastic bag and placed in water up to 1 metre / 3ft deep for hours [7] at low temperatures until just before being seared on a very hot pan. A second approach not involving bonding involves single piece of food being sealed inside a small silicone chamber, commonly known as a SV basket, and placed in boiling water for several minutes to achieve similar results [8] - although this latter technique requires having available separate equipment for steaming and seasoning afterward.

private placements or listings on stock exchanges that don't involve sales of existing assets to new investors provide faster growth than an IPO or merger, but carry significant risk. A stinky slINKY (also known as a slide rule) is a type of mathematical model used for solving linear programming problems, typically in game theory or economic analysis.

In a typical use of the slinky, the objective is to find the best strategy for two players to adopt with given information about each other. Ideally, this strategy will maximize their mutual gains without any restrictions on either player. The restriction commonly placed on both players is that they can’t know anything about each others' strategies; otherwise, they could both simply build their own optimal strategy and dominate the world! Players are told only that they have to choose between strategies of “neutral” strength against ones of “negative” strength against their opponent.

The concept of “stinkiness” comes from the mathematical definition of a global effective strategy, which implies a non-optimal strategy whereas a “stinky slinky” is a specialized type of global effective strategy. What's the difference between Texas Hold'em and Poker?

### Response:
generated_text:
Poker involves playing cards with other people, either in person or on video games like online poker. The goal is to be the best player who can make the highest value hand from cards worth 7 through Ace. You are initially given two decks of cards - one for you to keep and another which is given to the dealer. Each players starts with five cards, and then the game proceeds with two additional turns, during which time each player gets one more card (a "bet/fold") unless they are being played against, at which point the player is required to show their top three cards. 

The last player who bet during their turn either wins by having the most valuable hand after all hands are revealed, or else the money for the bet is returned plus interest to the previous owner of the winning hand. If there are no real winners, then the bet is a draw. 

Texas hold'em is the most common form of poker. It has two additional rules compared to all other forms of poker. In a standard tournament format, every player must announce their decision to "call" or "put down" before anyone reveals their hand. Second, once the flop has been announced (two new cards have been dealt after the bets), any remaining chips in play are removed and a new betting round begins after everyone has had an opportunity to reveal their first two cards. These two rule modifications help make Texas hold 'em more entertaining as compared to other variations like heads-up No Limit Hold'em.

A GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are processors designed for specialized computation used in graphical computing. They are very widely used today in things like computer graphics, artificial intelligence, data science, and quantum physics. GPUs were originally developed to accelerate the rendering of two-dimensional images, commonly seen in video games, but have since expanded to numerous other applications where computational efficiency and performance matter. 

As computing became more virtualized over the last few decades, CPUs (Central Processing Units) moved from being dedicated hardware to shared silicon through chip design companies partnering with software vendors. Much like how CPUs became part of a larger processing pipeline when working with data, GPUs act as intermediaries between algorithms and the data they're trying to solve. While CPU and neural network workloads had traditionally been separated on physical chips, increasingly both types of computations occur on the same processor cores, known as compute shaders in the case of GPUs. As some multi-pass tasks become intractable or even possible on CPUs (because of the complexity of the underlying problem), GPUs provide a faster and better solution with their billions of transistors designed specifically for high-performance calculation. By extension, this also means that many jobs that would once be executed on fast computers equipped with thousands of cores can now be performed much more efficiently on modern GPUs by spreading them across dozens or hundreds of smaller and more efficient cores. If you've played a recent game such as Call of Duty or Grand Theft Auto V, you've likely experienced what's known as a GPU-powered animation. These titles required years of development using the specialized processing abilities of modern GPUs.

Genomics is an approach to biological system analysis founded on the recognition that DNA, or genetic material,[h] makes up all living organisms and forms the basis of their distinct natures.[citation needed][4] In contrast to molecular biology, which seeks to understand individual genes and their functional consequences, genomics aims at structuring large sets of DNA sequences into functional grammars for biological systems and processes.[5] Genes themselves are often considered as units of genomic annotation, meaning that they can be referenced by a sequence identifier (e.g. SNP), and once identified are capable of being translated into function through epigenetic regulation or post-translational modifications. By itself, genome assembly represents only a first step toward understanding the functions of each gene in complex organisms.

These outputs must then be reassembled using various algorithms depending on the format (insertion/deletion-free, paired-end, transcriptional, etc.) and intended use. A notable example of such data reassembly is the Genomes2people project, established in 2001 with the goal of providing "biological context" to human genetics.

The power of genomics lies in its ability not merely to describe what genes do but also how these active ingredients interact within ecosystems of cells and tissues, allowing them to attain particular structures and perform specialized tasks. ### Instruction:
Why some believe that continuous optimisation problems might be easier to solve than discrete optimisation problems?

### Response:
generated_text:
First, let us say what is Continuous and Discrete Optimisation. In general, continuous optimisation represents any search problem whose objective value or target values are variable in time (i.e., the variables have non-zero realisations).  As opposed to this, discrete optimisation typically denotes a search problem where each variable has a fixed set of realizations R=C(0,..), with C being a non-empty sequence of constant fractions, such that for all i=1,..., r, o is in the range 0..1+c/r·T−τ−1 +. We can categorize continuous optimisation into two main categories: discrete one and state-controlling ones. State-Controlled Continuous Optimal Control is considered “easy” compared to discrete optimisation because if your objective function is given in its entirety at a particular time t, you can use some well known methods based on control charts or global optimisation policies to find a feasible solution. The challenges coming from state-controlled continuous optimal control are: firstly, for certain objectives equipped with negative weights, the convergence rate depends significantly on the initial value of the objective; secondly, the behaviour of the objective functions can depend on the context, e.g., when two different objective functions are allowed within a single search scenario (which results in overlapping sets of feasible solutions), how should we handle this information in our control charts?
Then there is another category of continuous optimisation: Non-Discrete Controlled Stop Levers which generally represents open-end or random search strategies for achieving minimax yields similarly complex behaviour as that of state-control methods, but cannot obtain consensus topologies as easily as state-control methods. The reason is that all candidates for a best stopping solution must be incorporated into the search graph, which causes the overall complexity of managing the search space to increase sharply.  On the other hand, according to Lucas et al., non-discrete controlled stop levers can still be classified as easy to medium among various method classes depending on their specificities. That is why many experts still think that discrete optimisation remains the most challenging class of large scale mechanical programming tasks. However, after 50 years of vigorous research by mathematicians, computer scientists, and engineers worldwide, they have also found some solid concrete techniques for solving these problems, through either exhaustive algorithms or control structures. It still takes professionals in this field very long times to tackle even moderate sized applications using currently available technology, although several new methods appear every year

This is what's known as fissile material - materials in which even a small amount of interaction can cause a high-impact reaction that releases massive amounts of heat and energy. Nuclear fusion, on the other hand, is really cool. If two hydrogen nuclei bond over their shared lightness (or electron density) they combine to form deuterium/tritium, which has a half-life of 2 years and emits 3 times more radiation than helium-4 after 10 days but doesn't contain any neutrons which may interfere with stable isotopes so it's pretty much self-sustaining. For any program f that might determine whether programs halt, a "pathological" program g, called with some input, can pass its own source and its input to f and then specifically do the opposite of what f predicts g will do. No f can exist that handles this case. A key part of the proof is a mathematical definition of a computer and program, which is known as a Turing machine; the halting problem is undecidable over Turing machines. It is one of the first cases of decision problems proven to be unsolvable. This proof is significant to practical computing efforts, defining a class of applications which no programming invention can possibly perform perfectly.

### Response:

Smaller deletions result in Microdeletion syndrome, which are detected using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)

For example, a noun is normally defined as the naming element which appears before its function in a sentence, e.g. John stepped up to the plate. Nouns can also have particles attached, such as attributive adjectives (typically indicating a special character or aspect of something) or nominal participles (usually stating the number of times the item has been named). There are some exceptions, such as prepositions, which typically occur before their position in a sentence. Real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems are specialist money transfer systems where funds transfers "real time" and in most cases on a 'one world' basis. India being the largest importer/exporter in the world, with huge amounts of fund transfers across both channels each year, has created a robust institutional framework facilitating such activities and thus far maintained stability without the need to create a separate national institution for this purpose. ### Instruction:
What is a Synchronous Concurrent Algorithm (SCA)?

### Response:
generated_text:
In computer science, a Synchronous Concurrent Algorithm (or SCA) is an algorithm that simultaneously executes multiple commands and receives update estimates for each command from some external source, usually a global clock. The updates are synchronously transmitted to all of the agent's implementing parts; they do not execute simultaneously in any one place. All concurrent algorithms share two fundamental properties: mutual exclusion - if part A computes F(x), part B cannot concurrently determine F(x + 1) or F(x)/F(x + 2). First-order algorithms obey this property unless specific limits on synchronization speeds are violated. Second, agents are responsible for communicating their actual computations to the receiving side, i.e., they "report" their results rather than passively receiving updated calculations as they go along.

The basic design pattern of synchronous computational engines consists of having some front end manage some centralized state, some agents running remote but parallel applications, and some form of synchronization media transmitting individual updates or reports to every agent. The design of SCAs is often simplified by using high-level coordination schemes to enforce mutual cancellation and consistency of data representations.

### Instruction:
Should generative AI be banned from the classroom?

The idea of banning Generative AI in the classroom, seems absurd and ridiculous at first glance. But, when we look closely at what it means to train generative models and why these models can sometimes produce content that is offensively racist or sexist, we can see how this technology could cause harm and contribute to a culture of sexism and unfairness in our schools and education system. To train these models, you have to give them huge datasets of images, Videos and text. Most of these materials come from users and are entirely offensive or biased. This can lead to unintended biases in the system which may then propagate across the entire educational ecosystem and further reinforce harmful norms or stereotypes. In finance, a derivative is a contract that derives its value from the performance of an underlying entity. A key advantage of derivatives over simple forward contracts is that they allow holders to benefit from price changes (a synthetic position) without having to physically assume the risks of the underlying movement. Another notable asymmetric feature of certain derivative transactions is the ability of one party to end the contract unilaterally at any time; this creates what is commonly known as a "time disparity" between the upside and downside exposures held by buyers and sellers. As these and other features have encouraged more speculative use of derivates, regulators across the world have been implementing rules intended to reduce systemic risk generated by these markets, including by requiring market participants to post higher levels of cash or highly rated securities as collateral.

Water whose ORP reaches 1 is completely evaporated into steam; this kind of dehydrated vapor is technically dubbed hypercooled water. Hypercooled water with an ORP above 1 is rare but does exist. ORPs greater than 1 indicate that the water molecules are very tightly packed together, their distance apart is significantly less than 1 electron charge per water molecule, aka they are very wet. Modern pacemakers usually have multiple functions. The most basic form monitors the heart's native electrical rhythm. When the pacemaker wire or "lead" does not detect heart electrical activity in the chamber – atrium or ventricle – within a normal beat-to-beat time period – most commonly one second – it will stimulate either the atrium or the ventricle with a short low voltage pulse. If it does sense electrical activity, it will hold off stimulating. This sensing and stimulating activity continues on a beat by beat basis and is called "demand pacing". In the case of a dual-chamber device, when the upper chambers have a spontaneous or stimulated activation, the device starts a countdown to ensure that in an acceptable – and programmable – interval, there is an activation of the ventricle, otherwise again an impulse will be delivered.

Therefore the stress will increase above what it was initially before any compression occurred. Note however, there is no longer any ratio between stress and strain because the latter is negative.

### Instruction:
What is the Monty Hall problem?

### Response:
generated_text:
The Monty Hall problem, named after the game show host who devised it, is considered the most difficult probability brain teaser in modern mathematics. The problem states that a contestant has been selected to try to win a prize. Before the show begins, the host shows three doors, one of which is locked and cannot be opened. The host allows the contestant to pick one of the other two doors as a first selection. Then, during the course of the program, the host opens one of the remaining doors so that the contestant can see that it is not the locked door. The host now requires the participant to decide whether to switch their initial selection, which they have chosen, to the still-locked door or keep their original selection and bet on the remaining unopened door being the prize. What is required is a decision calculus equation describing the optimal strategy.

There are many combinatorial formulations of the Monty Hall Problem, relating to scenarios with more than three options or where switching does or does not improve your chance of winning the prize. Every such formulation is challenging but some are easier to solve than others. John Martin Fischer, Alonzo Church, and Dennis Parness Goodchild each developed resolutions to these problems using novel algebraic techniques. It remains challenging to understand exactly how much information is required for optimal choice and what factors/motivations should be considered.

Start Early and Share Your Vision
Getting everyone on the same page and sharing your vision upfront will help you streamline the process and make sure nobody misses any important details. Design an Effective Process

Ensure Everyone Gains Enough Access

The key distinction in civil liability arising out of negligence or breach of contract is between laches (time bar) and waiver (foregoing of right).

For instance, let's say you are constructing a building which suffered irreparable damage because the builder neglected to properly reinforce one of the new construction's walls. As a result, a large piece of brick suddenly fell down, injuring someone below. An action may be brought against the builder for damages resulting from the injuries caused by lapse of builder's duty. The issue will then arise whether the delay or the omission formed the basis for letting the plaintiff thrive without defense.

To prevail on laches, it is not enough for the plaintiff to show that he was actually injured due to the defendant's actions; the plaintiff must also Show that if he had been aware of the circumstances occurring before the injury took place, he would have exercised the same degree of care as a reasonable man would have done. Given that construction projects often take longer than expected, and there might have been deviations from optimal schedule, the standard of reasonable expectation might well be higher than what a typical buyer would expect, requiring the plaintiff to prove both absence of fault and substantial damages.

On the other hand, under waiver, the failure to exercise ordinary care does not estop the defendant from defending itself based on the assumption that the plaintiff knew or should have known of all hazards which were part of the transaction, and chose to engage in it nonetheless. A common example where someone else exercises discretionary control over another person is that of a driver who accepts delivery of a car with a broken brake light or flat tire. ### Instruction:
What is proteomics?

### Response:
generated_text:
Proteomics refers to the large-scale study of proteins. Proteins are vital parts of living cells, with many functions such as chemical synthesis, metabolism, receptor signaling, and cell differentiation.[15] Although DNA sequences constitute genes for protein production and structural modification,[16][17] it is only the nucleic acid sequence that provides the "programming" for the biological process; the actual production of the desired protein requires other molecular mechanisms, at least in part initiated by the gene product itself or by enzymes associated with it. Indeed, evidence suggests that most of genome is not actively transcribed but instead serves primarily to store and transmit genetic information via RNA molecules.[18][19]

For these reasons, understanding a protein's structure (and, more recently, its function) is crucial for understanding how that protein works within a biological system. Thus, the field of proteomics specializes in the large-scale identification, extraction, and analysis of proteins from biological fluids and tissues. This offers valuable insight into various diseases and human disorders, including aging and disease. Progress has been made through combination of methods such as mass spectrometry, high throughput screening, and two-dimensional surface protein analysis using experimental imaging technology (crystallography). The resulting data sets are immense, often covering hundreds of millions of proteins separated by nanomsites on a microplate. Analysis pipeline typically include data cleaning, signal processing and visualization.

The proteome is the complete set of proteins produced or modified by a particular organism or cellular process. Since proteomes differ between organisms, species, tissues, cells types, and developmental stages, this term is used also to describe different levels of proteolytic digestion (a process which purifies a complex sample such as a mammalian plasma or urine to isolate specific proteins). Furthermore, various sources have further expanded the definition of proteomics to include non-protein molecules such as peptide fragments and small oligomers. These larger samples allow for higher resolution studies of particular protein subtypes or protein pathways.

Finally, proteomics may be applied in basic research to understand processes like proteinogenesis, enzyme activity, post-translational modifications, and protein-protein interactions. It can also be used in drug discovery by identifying potential targets for therapeutic interventions or disease biomarkers. One example is the Human Proteomics Research Pipeline initiative at Stanford University, created by student Taylor Harris and professor Gerhard Wagner who developed a standardized protocol for parallel fractionation of whole blood into extractions for both protein analysis and sequencing.

### Instruction:
What is geomorphometry?

### Response:
generated_text: Geomorphometry, or morphometrics (although generally geomorphological data are not considered to be "morphometric"), combines geometric theory with topographic information in order to characterize the shape of landforms and their variability. Common geometric assumptions are Euclidean geometry and that the landform shape depends only on height and latitude/longitude coordinates. Topography however often affects hydrology, vegetation, soil composition and many other phenomena and therefore has implications beyond the basic description of the landform shape; for these reasons more sophisticated representations are used which may include contributions from geometric constraints as well as the underlying terrain. Landform shape in turn can affect many different applications ranging from control of infrastructure – e.g., flood management networks – to assessment of habitat suitability for wildlife species. Geomorphometric software packages typically include tools for collection, processing and analysis of elevation series (typically lidar), geographical information system ("GIS") output, and also vector landform shapes such as raster images. The most applied geometric approaches within this field tend to fall into two broad categories: spatial derivative functions (referred to either "linear regression" when based upon linear relationships between points, or otherwise "non-linear") and generalization of basic geometric relationships termed algebraic transforms. Spatial derivatives allow simple separation of features according to the direction of movement (e.g., slope) and some degree of time delay, providing a resolution sufficient for evaluation over small areas. Generalized algebraic transform (GT) methodology allows more complex interactions to occur among features and provides the basis for algorithms incorporating various types of statistical information as well as mathematical modelling and computer simulation. Common applications range from automated detection of landforms/landscape structures at scale across both natural and artificial sources using both image-based and ground-based sensing techniques, through validation and interpretation of survey results, to identification of patterns in hydrology, deposition, erosion etc... With increasing availability of high-resolution landsurface datasets of greater detail worldwide coupled with increased computation power available to data analysts, practitioners have become increasingly interested in applying geomorphometry to a wider variety of scientific, policy-related and business needs.
